description: Short, continuously updated plain-language overview of where ME/CFS research stands, shown on the dashboard's Overview tab and rendered to STATE-OF-THE-ART.md. It is a synthesis of the confirmed entries in data/papers.json and data/trials.json — every point cites their ids in `refs`, and nothing may be claimed that those entries do not support. STYLE: layperson language as in papers.json and the writing rules in ROUTINE.md (no dashes as punctuation, no stock phrases); one-sentence `takeaway` per section; 2–6 `points` per section, each ≤ ~45 words; replace outdated points rather than appending. `confidence` is one of: established, strong, emerging, contested, early. Bump a section's `updated` (and top-level `updated`) only when its content changes; set top-level `reviewed` every run. Optional `keywords` (lower-case substrings matched against paper titles + summaries) assign papers to a section's topic for the Papers-tab topic filter; cited `refs` are always included. See ROUTINE.md → 'State of the art'. Also holds `model` (the 'how it may fit together' diagram: rows of nodes, each linked to a section) and `treatments` (the treatment board: result = promising | negative | testing, a short `note`, cited `refs`); keep both in sync with the sections. Each section has a `short_title` for its tile.
intro: A short summary in plain language of what research shows about ME/CFS so far. It only uses the papers and trials listed on this site and is updated when new results come in.

model.title: How the pieces may fit together
model.caption: This is one leading model, proposed by Wirth and Scheibenbogen. Some steps are well supported, others are still being tested, and it may not fit every patient.

sections.title: What ME/CFS is
sections.takeaway: A serious, long-lasting physical illness. Its main feature is a crash after even small amounts of activity.

points.text: The main symptom is post-exertional malaise (PEM). After physical or mental effort, symptoms get much worse, often with a delay. Current diagnostic criteria are built around it.
PEM can be measured. In two exercise tests 24 hours apart, patients cannot repeat their performance from the first day.
Depending on the definition, roughly 0.5 to 1% of people worldwide have ME/CFS.
Many cases start after an infection. In a large New York survey, about one in five people reported PEM after COVID-19, and post-COVID patients come to look more and more like ME/CFS over time.
International experts have agreed on a common way to measure the core symptoms. That makes studies easier to compare.

sections.title: Genes
sections.takeaway: Large genetic studies show that ME/CFS has an inherited part, mainly involving the nervous and immune systems.

points.text: DecodeME is the largest genetic study so far, with more than 15,000 patients. It found eight DNA regions linked to ME/CFS, several of them involved in fighting infection.
Other groups have found the same gene hits in other data. The strongest signals are in genes for the brain and nerve signals, not in the blood.

ME/CFS seems to have its own genetic roots in nerve cells. It is not a form of depression, even if some symptoms overlap. In people followed after an infection, inherited depression risk did not predict who developed a CFS-like illness.
Genetic cause-and-effect analyses point to cellular energy production, low-grade inflammation and clotting as likely causes of the illness, not just results of it.

sections.title: Immune system & autoantibodies
sections.takeaway: The immune system is clearly involved. Self-attacking antibodies are a leading theory, but removing them has had mixed results so far.

points.text: Many patients have autoantibodies against receptors that control blood vessels and nerves. These are antibodies that attack the body's own receptors. A similar pattern shows up when the illness followed an infection and, less often, a vaccination. Scheibenbogen's autoimmune model is based on this.
Lab studies show that these antibodies can do harm. Patients' antibodies damaged the energy machinery of cells, and antibodies from long-COVID patients caused symptoms in mice.
The first line of immune defence (innate immunity) tends to overreact. A calcium channel in immune cells called TRPM3 is faulty, and several labs have confirmed this.

Immunoadsorption filters antibodies out of the blood. In a German post-COVID trial it lowered antibody levels but did no better than a sham procedure, and a second small study was also negative. Two studies in Berlin are still following it in antibody-positive patients.

Removing B cells with rituximab failed in a large trial. Targeting the plasma cells that make antibodies with daratumumab helped 6 of 10 patients in a small pilot. Charité is planning a placebo-controlled B-cell trial with inebilizumab.

sections.title: Blood vessels & circulation
sections.takeaway: Small blood vessels that work poorly and disturbed blood flow are among the most consistent findings.

points.text: The inner lining of the blood vessels (endothelium) works poorly in many patients. A simple eye test showed this most clearly in post-COVID patients who meet ME/CFS criteria.
During exercise, too little blood returns to the heart (preload failure), and the muscles have trouble using the oxygen they get.
Dizziness and a racing heart when standing (orthostatic intolerance, POTS) are common. In one study, more than a third of teenagers with ME/CFS had POTS.
It is unclear whether low blood volume is behind this. Wirth thinks so, but a recent study that measured blood volume found it made no difference.

Microclots are tiny clots that are hard to dissolve and may block small vessels. They have been found in long COVID and ME/CFS. Lab evidence is growing, but none of the trials listed here targets them yet.

sections.title: Muscles & energy
sections.takeaway: Muscles and the energy supply of cells are affected. This is where the Wirth and Scheibenbogen drug MDC002 comes in.

points.text: The theory of Wirth and Scheibenbogen: with too little blood flow, sodium and then calcium build up in muscle cells. This damages their power plants (mitochondria) and causes the crash after activity.
Muscle samples from patients look different from those of healthy people after 60 days of bed rest, so the changes are not just from inactivity.
Blood tests point to a low-energy survival mode and a blocked step in turning food into energy. Brain scans show extra lactate, a sign that energy is being made without enough oxygen.
Not every result holds up. A careful repeat of a well-known study found no factor in patients' blood that harms healthy muscle cells.
MDC002 from Klaus Wirth's company Mitodicure is designed to break this cycle of calcium overload in muscle. A first trial in humans is planned but not registered yet.

sections.title: Brain & nervous system
sections.takeaway: Brain scans and spinal-fluid tests show measurable changes. Which of them drive the illness is still unclear.

points.text: Part of the fatigue seems to start in the brain. When muscles tire, the brain normally sends a stronger signal to make up for it. In ME/CFS this signal hardly rises.
Brain chemistry is changed. Spinal fluid shows too little noradrenaline activity, a messenger for alertness, and the stress hormone cortisol is low.
The brain's cleaning system during sleep seems weaker. That fits with poor sleep and brain fog.
It is not settled whether there is inflammation in the brain. An older scan study found signs of it. A recent post-COVID study found no immune attack in the brain.

sections.title: Viruses & triggers
sections.takeaway: Infections and dormant viruses that become active again are likely triggers. Antiviral treatment has not helped so far.

points.text: Common dormant viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and HHV-6 often become active again during severe COVID-19. This has been linked to later long COVID.
Pieces of the coronavirus have been found in the gut tissue of people with long COVID.
But the largest antiviral trial, with Paxlovid, showed no benefit. A drug against proteins from old virus sequences in our DNA (temelimab) also failed.

sections.title: Gut
sections.takeaway: Gut problems are common and go along with more severe illness. Treating the gut is an early idea that makes sense.

points.text: About one in three patients also has irritable bowel syndrome. Worse gut symptoms go with worse ME/CFS symptoms and more inflammation.
Patients lack some helpful gut bacteria, including ones that make a fuel for the gut lining.
In a small placebo-controlled trial, a probiotic reduced fatigue in long COVID. It needs to be repeated with more people.

sections.title: Tests & biomarkers
sections.takeaway: There is still no validated lab test for ME/CFS, but several candidates look promising.

points.text: The most advanced candidates are blood tests based on how DNA is folded (96% accuracy in one test group) and on RNA fragments in the blood (about 77%). Both need wider testing.
Large studies of blood proteins and of tiny particles released by cells find consistent differences. Some of this work comes from Scheibenbogen's group.
Simple physical tests such as repeated grip-strength measurements show real weakness and could track the effect of treatment. On their own they cannot diagnose ME/CFS.
Patients seem to fall into subgroups, for example a group with heavier symptoms that more often started after an infection. How to define these groups reliably is still open.

sections.title: Treatment: what has been tested
sections.takeaway: There is no approved drug for ME/CFS yet. Some ideas show early promise, and several well-run trials were negative.

points.text: Early positive signals: BC007, which blocks autoantibodies, in a placebo-controlled long-COVID trial; daratumumab in a small pilot; and hyperbaric oxygen in a Charité study without placebo group. All of them need confirmation.
Negative or disappointing: rituximab, Paxlovid, temelimab, immunoadsorption compared with a sham procedure, and repurposed drugs that brought only a small benefit that did not last.

Exercise programmes can ease some symptoms but do not improve physical capacity, and patients rate graded exercise therapy as least helpful. In a Charité trial, better-organised care alone did not improve function.
Trials often miss what patients actually use. Only about 1 in 14 registered post-COVID trials tests a treatment that patients rely on, and few use PEM as the main outcome.

sections.title: Trials to watch in Germany
sections.takeaway: Several German drug studies are open or planned. The Studies tab lists who can take part.

points.text: Open now: bupropion for post-COVID fatigue at up to 11 university hospitals, and two immunoadsorption studies for antibody-positive patients in Berlin and Potsdam.
Planned at Charité: B-cell therapy with inebilizumab for patients who improved after immunoadsorption and then relapsed, and low-dose aripiprazole.
Planned by Mitodicure (Klaus Wirth): the first study of MDC002 in humans.
